衡量医疗 AI 实际能做什么

inlines.text: 衡量医疗 AI 实际能做什么

blocks.text: 日期
主题
基础模型医疗健康
在三年多的时间里，我们为医疗 AI 构建了难度逐步提升、越来越贴近现实的基准测试。以下是我们得到的经验。

inlines.text: 在三年多的时间里，我们为医疗 AI 构建了难度逐步提升、越来越贴近现实的基准测试。以下是我们得到的经验。

blocks.text: 大型语言模型如今在医师资格考试中几乎拿到满分，这激发了人们对 AI 在医疗健康领域潜力的热情。但在一场多项选择题考试中拿高分，和在医疗系统中工作，是完全不同的两回事。资格考试要求你给出正确答案。而医疗系统要求你打开病历、找到两年前的超声心动图、将其与今早的化验结果核对、决定该怎么做、下达医嘱，并写好病历记录。前者考查知识。后者考查你能否跨越时间、文档和软件系统完成许多任务。如果我们想知道 AI 在临床上是否有用，就必须用实际处理的任务来评估它。

inlines.text: 大型语言模型如今在医师资格考试中几乎拿到满分，这激发了人们对 AI 在医疗健康领域潜力的热情。但在一场多项选择题考试中拿高分，和在医疗系统中工作，是完全不同的两回事。资格考试要求你给出正确答案。而医疗系统要求你打开病历、找到两年前的超声心动图、将其与今早的化验结果核对、决定该怎么做、下达医嘱，并写好病历记录。前者考查知识。后者考查你能否跨越时间、文档和软件系统完成许多任务。如果我们想知道 AI 在临床上是否有用，就必须用实际处理的任务来评估它。

blocks.text: 正是这种区别，推动了我们三年多来为医疗 AI 构建难度逐步提升、越来越贴近现实的基准测试的工作。我们从 MedHELM 开始，这是一项系统性工作，旨在梳理临床任务的全貌，并衡量当今最好的模型在这些任务上的表现。随后我们通过 PhysicianBench 进一步深入，它测试 AI 智能体能否在可运行的电子健康记录环境中端到端完成真实的临床任务；还有 HealthAdminBench，它探索行政管理和工作流程。

inlines.text: 正是这种区别，推动了我们三年多来为医疗 AI 构建难度逐步提升、越来越贴近现实的基准测试的工作。我们从 MedHELM 开始，这是一项系统性工作，旨在梳理临床任务的全貌，并衡量当今最好的模型在这些任务上的表现。随后我们通过 PhysicianBench 进一步深入，它测试 AI 智能体能否在可运行的电子健康记录环境中端到端完成真实的临床任务；还有 HealthAdminBench，它探索行政管理和工作流程。

blocks.text: 这些基准测试讲述了同一个故事：当今最好的 AI 智能体完成的工作不到一半。智能体在跨步骤、文档和系统移动时会丢失信息。

inlines.text: 这些基准测试讲述了同一个故事：当今最好的 AI 智能体完成的工作不到一半。智能体在跨步骤、文档和系统移动时会丢失信息。

blocks.text: 在本文中，我们解释我们如何构建这些测试、发现了什么，以及要弥合 AI 声称能做的事与实际所做的事之间的差距需要付出什么。

blocks.text: MedHELM：梳理整个工作
2023 年，在 MedAlign 中，15 位临床医生编写了 983 个他们会向患者病历提出的问题。当时最好的模型 GPT-4 在其 35% 的回复中产生了错误，这促使我们在 2024 年初构建了 MedHELM。

inlines.text: 中，15 位临床医生编写了 983 个他们会向患者病历提出的问题。当时最好的模型 GPT-4 在其 35% 的回复中产生了错误，这促使我们在 2024 年初构建了 MedHELM。

blocks.text: MedHELM 是我们尝试系统性地开展基于任务的评估的成果。我们从需要完成的工作或任务出发，再围绕这些任务设计测试。在 29 位临床医生的参与下，我们构建了一个分类体系，包含 5 个类别、22 个子类别和 121 项任务，反映了医疗照护提供中常见的工作。这些类别包括临床决策支持、临床记录生成、患者沟通与教育、医学研究辅助，以及行政与工作流（图 1）。

blocks.text: 任务是工作流
MedHELM 基准评测的是单次回复：输入一个提示，输出文本，然后对文本评分。两个薄弱类别中的真实任务很少是这个样子。

inlines.text: MedHELM 基准评测的是单次回复：输入一个提示，输出文本，然后对文本评分。两个薄弱类别中的真实任务很少是这个样子。

blocks.text: 事先授权就是一个很好的例子。有人要在 EHR（电子健康记录）中读取医嘱，核对支付方的标准，调取支持性文档，填写门户表单，附加文件，提交，并在病历中记录参考编号。专科会诊也是同样的形态：跨多次就诊检索数据，对其推理，开具医嘱，并记录。对模型在第 3 步会生成的文本进行评分，完全无法说明第 7 步是否会发生。

blocks.text: 对于这些重要类别，我们需要一种不同的评估方式。给智能体一个环境、一个目标和一些工具。让它行动。然后检查环境中发生了什么变化。这正是 PhysicianBench（探索临床决策支持与执行）和 HealthAdminBench（探索行政与工作流）背后的设计思路。

blocks.text: PhysicianBench 与 MedAgentBench：AI 智能体能完成临床工作吗？

inlines.text: PhysicianBench 与 MedAgentBench：AI 智能体能完成临床工作吗？

blocks.text: MedAgentBench 建立了 300 个患者特定的临床衍生任务，涵盖 10 个类别，由人类医生编写。这些任务基于虚拟电子健康记录计算环境中 100 名患者的真实档案。当该基准于 2025 年初发布时，即使是最好的前沿模型也仅能完成不到 70% 的任务。到 2026 年，智能体技术的进步使得前沿模型的任务完成率超过 90%。

blocks.text: PhysicianBench 进一步拓展前沿，包含 100 个长周期、多步骤任务，改编自初级保健医生与专科医生之间的真实医疗咨询，覆盖 21 个专科。一个独立的医生小组独立审查了每个任务。这些任务在 EHR 沙盒中针对合成重建的患者记录进行尝试。一个平均的多步骤任务需要 27 次工具调用。

blocks.text: 总体而言，评估任务结果共产生 670 项检查，涵盖数据检索、临床推理、操作执行和文档记录。评分基于执行结果：任务特定脚本检查记录中是否存在正确的医嘱，并对推理和笔记进行 LLM 评判。

blocks.text: 在 12 个模型中，表现最好的（GPT-5.5）在单次尝试中完成了 46% 的任务。最好的开源模型 DeepSeek V4-Pro 达到了 19%。一致性更差：GPT-5.5 在其全部三次运行中仅正确执行了 28% 的任务。

blocks.text: 失败分析给了我们更多洞察，临床推理中仍然存在局限性，约占失败检查点的一半。错误主要是推理不完整和接近正确，而完全错误的结论很少见。此外，还有一种过去任何基准都无法捕捉的失败。在操作执行失败中，GPT-5.5 的 62% 和 Claude Opus 4.6 的 73% 是智能体在笔记中写下了正确的操作，却从未在 EHR 中下达医嘱。AI 生成了文笔优美的文字，形成了良好的计划，但从未真正完成工作。

blocks.text: HealthAdminBench：AI 智能体能做非临床工作吗？

inlines.text: HealthAdminBench：AI 智能体能做非临床工作吗？

blocks.text: HealthAdminBench 针对医疗系统的大部分工作和人员配置：每次患者就诊背后发生的计费、授权和行政工作。幕后行政人员的数量正在快速增长，可能已经以 10:1 的比例超过一线临床医生。我们花了 100 多个小时观察斯坦福医疗保健的行政人员，以构建四个模拟网络环境：一个 EHR、两个付款方门户和一个传真系统。AI 智能体能够像人一样通过截图、点击和打字来操作它们。

blocks.text: 综合解读这些基准
这些基准做出了互补的押注。PhysicianBench 优先关注基于真实临床记录的、面向临床医生流程的保真度。HealthAdminBench 优先关注在医疗系统中大量行政流程上对人类工作流程的复现。

inlines.text: 这些基准做出了互补的押注。PhysicianBench 优先关注基于真实临床记录的、面向临床医生流程的保真度。HealthAdminBench 优先关注在医疗系统中大量行政流程上对人类工作流程的复现。

Measuring What Medical AI Can Actually Do

inlines.text: Measuring What Medical AI Can Actually Do

blocks.text: Date
October 19, 2026
Topics
Foundation ModelsHealthcare
Over three years, we’ve built progressively harder, more realistic benchmarks for medical AI. Here’s what we learned.

inlines.text: Over three years, we’ve built progressively harder, more realistic benchmarks for medical AI. Here’s what we learned.

blocks.text: Large language models now score near-perfect on medical licensing exams, fueling enthusiasm about AI’s potential in healthcare. But acing a multiple-choice test and working in a health system are very different things. A licensing exam asks for the right answer. A health system asks you to open a chart, find the echocardiogram from two years ago, reconcile it with this morning’s labs, decide what to do, place the orders, and write the note. One tests knowledge. The other tests whether you can do many tasks across time, documents, and software systems. If we want to know whether AI is clinically useful, we have to evaluate it on the tasks actually handled.

inlines.text: Large language models now score near-perfect on medical licensing exams, fueling enthusiasm about AI’s potential in healthcare. But acing a multiple-choice test and working in a health system are very different things. A licensing exam asks for the right answer. A health system asks you to open a chart, find the echocardiogram from two years ago, reconcile it with this morning’s labs, decide what to do, place the orders, and write the note. One tests knowledge. The other tests whether you can do many tasks across time, documents, and software systems. If we want to know whether AI is clinically useful, we have to evaluate it on the tasks actually handled.

blocks.text: That distinction is what drove our three years of work building progressively harder, more realistic benchmarks for medical AI. We started with MedHELM, a systematic effort to map the full landscape of clinical tasks and measure how today’s best models perform across them. Then we went deeper with PhysicianBench, which tests whether AI agents can complete real clinical tasks end-to-end inside a functioning electronic health record environment, and HealthAdminBench, which explores administration and workflow.

inlines.text: That distinction is what drove our three years of work building progressively harder, more realistic benchmarks for medical AI. We started with MedHELM, a systematic effort to map the full landscape of clinical tasks and measure how today’s best models perform across them. Then we went deeper with PhysicianBench, which tests whether AI agents can complete real clinical tasks end-to-end inside a functioning electronic health record environment, and HealthAdminBench, which explores administration and workflow.

blocks.text: These benchmarks tell the same story: Today’s best AI agents complete less than half the work. Agents lose track of information as they move across steps, documents, and systems.

blocks.text: In this post, we explain how we built these tests, what we found, and what it will take to close the gap between what AI says it can do and what it actually does.

blocks.text: MedHELM: Mapping the Whole Job

In 2023, in MedAlign, 15 clinicians wrote 983 questions of the kind they would pose to a patient’s record. The best model at the time, GPT-4, produced errors in 35% of its responses, which led us to build MedHELM in early 2024.

inlines.text: , 15 clinicians wrote 983 questions of the kind they would pose to a patient’s record. The best model at the time, GPT-4, produced errors in 35% of its responses, which led us to build MedHELM in early 2024.

blocks.text: MedHELM was our attempt to systematically conduct a task-based evaluation. We started with the jobs or tasks to be done, and then designed the tests around them. With input from 29 clinicians, we built a taxonomy with five categories, 22 subcategories, and 121 tasks reflecting commonly done work in delivering medical care. The categories included clinical decision support, clinical note generation, patient communication and education, medical research assistance, and administration and workflow (Figure 1).

blocks.text: Models consistently struggled on clinical decision support and administration and workflow tasks, exactly where health systems actually want the most help to address clinician time and administrative cost. Administrative spending in the U.S. alone exceeds $1 trillion a year. The categories with the largest potential return scored the lowest.

blocks.text: Tasks Are Workflows
MedHELM benchmarks grade single responses: A prompt goes in, text comes out, and the text is scored. Real tasks in the two weak categories rarely look like that.

inlines.text: MedHELM benchmarks grade single responses: A prompt goes in, text comes out, and the text is scored. Real tasks in the two weak categories rarely look like that.

blocks.text: A prior authorization is a good example. Someone reads the order in the EHR (electronic health record), checks the payer’s criteria, pulls supporting documentation, fills out a portal form, attaches files, submits, and records the reference number in the chart. A specialist consult has the same shape: retrieve data across encounters, reason about it, place orders, and document. Grading the text a model would produce at step 3 tells you nothing about whether step 7 happens.

blocks.text: We need a different kind of evaluation for these important categories. Give an agent an environment, a goal, and tools. Let it act. Then check what changed in the environment. That is the design behind PhysicianBench, which explores clinical decision support and execution, and HealthAdminBench, which explores administration and workflow.

blocks.text: PhysicianBench and MedAgentBench: Can AI Agents Do the Clinical Work?

inlines.text: PhysicianBench and MedAgentBench: Can AI Agents Do the Clinical Work?

blocks.text: MedAgentBench established 300 patient-specific clinically derived tasks across 10 categories, written by human physicians. The tasks are based on realistic profiles of 100 patients in a virtual electronic health record compute environment. When this was released in early 2025, even the best frontier models achieved <70% proper task completion. By 2026, agentic advances are now seeing frontier models with over 90% task completion.

blocks.text: PhysicianBench pushes the frontiers further with 100 long-horizon, multi-step tasks adapted from real medical consultations between primary care physicians and subspecialists, across 21 specialties. A separate panel of physicians independently reviewed each task. The tasks are attempted against synthetically reconstructed patient records in an EHR sandbox. An average multi-step task takes 27 tool calls.

blocks.text: Across 12 models, the best (GPT-5.5) completed 46% of tasks on a single attempt. The best open-source model, DeepSeek V4-Pro, reached 19%. Consistency is worse: GPT-5.5 properly executed only 28% of tasks in all three of its runs.

blocks.text: Failure analysis gives us even more insight, as there are still limitations in clinical reasoning that account for about half of the failed checkpoints. The errors are mostly incomplete reasoning and near misses, while outright wrong conclusions are rare. In addition, there is a failure that no past benchmark could catch. Among action-execution failures, 62% for GPT-5.5 and 73% for Claude Opus 4.6 were cases where the agent wrote the correct action in its note and never placed the order in the EHR. The AI generated beautifully written words into a good plan, but never actually got the work done.

blocks.text: HealthAdminBench: Can AI Agents Do the Non-Clinical Work?

inlines.text: HealthAdminBench: Can AI Agents Do the Non-Clinical Work?

blocks.text: HealthAdminBench targets the bulk of healthcare system effort and staffing: the billing, authorization, and administrative work that happens behind the scenes of every patient encounter. The number of behind-the-scenes administrative staff is rapidly growing and may already outnumber frontline clinicians 10:1. We spent more than 100 hours observing administrators at Stanford Health Care to build four simulated web environments, an EHR, two payer portals, and a fax system. AI agents are able to operate them the way a person would, through screenshots, clicks, and typing.

blocks.text: There are 135 tasks across three workflows (60 prior authorizations, 60 appeals and denials, 15 durable medical equipment orders) at three difficulty levels, designed with practicing administrators. Each task decomposes into subtasks, and 1,698 verifiers grade them: 1,177 deterministic checks and 521 LLM-judge rubrics. All patient data is synthetic, allowing us to release the environments and run a leaderboard for public use.

All patient data is synthetic, allowing us to release the environments and run a leaderboard for public use.

blocks.text: The best agent tested at the time, Claude Opus 4.6 in its native computer-use mode, completed 36.3% of tasks end-to-end. The best open-weight model, Kimi K2.5, completed 15.6%.

blocks.text: A key distinction is that GPT-5.4 in computer-use mode passed 82.8% of individual subtasks but completed only 26.7% of whole tasks. Competence on the parts does not add up to reliability in a whole workflow. Filling out a form, then sending it to the wrong address doesn’t count. Patients aren’t going to grant partial credit for completing the documentation while prescribing the wrong medicine.

blocks.text: Here, the failures are coordination failures. Agents gather information in the EHR that they will need much later in a payer portal, fail to write it down, and lose it. They miss file uploads and downloads even when the task requires them. They rarely go back to fix an earlier step, and run out of budget instead.

blocks.text: Reading the Benches Together

These benchmarks make complementary bets. PhysicianBench prioritizes fidelity around clinician-facing processes based on real clinical records. HealthAdminBench prioritizes replication of human workflows for extensive administrative processes in healthcare systems.

inlines.text: These benchmarks make complementary bets. PhysicianBench prioritizes fidelity around clinician-facing processes based on real clinical records. HealthAdminBench prioritizes replication of human workflows for extensive administrative processes in healthcare systems.

blocks.text: A health system governing AI adoption needs both kinds of applications, with evidence for reproducibility and transparency marked by release of (synthetic) data, public code, and leaderboards.

inlines.text: A health system governing AI adoption needs both kinds of applications, with evidence for reproducibility and transparency marked by release of (synthetic) data, public code, and leaderboards.

blocks.text: The headline performance of 46% task completion in PhysicianBench is not directly comparable with 36% task completion in HealthAdminBench. The environments, model sets, interfaces, and grading schemes differ. The defensible claim is directional: Two independently built, execution-grounded benchmarks, one clinical and one administrative, both find today’s best agents finishing less than half of the work. In both, the dominant failures come from failing to carry information across encounters, documents, and systems, which points to agent architecture and memory (i.e., better harnesses) as the fix, at least as much as bigger models.

blocks.text: Both benchmarks trace back to the categories in which MedHELM found the weakest performance. MedHELM (www.medhelm.org) is community-owned and released under an Apache 2.0 license, and the point of an open framework is that others can contribute category-specific, workflow-level benchmarks. In fact, we are contributing both HealthAdminBench and PhysicianBench. If your health system has a workflow that matters and a benchmark to test it, we invite you to contribute it to MedHELM.
